A.title: A
A.text:
Saturday at Fenwick Mill
The old mill is opening its doors to people who would like to see how grain becomes flour. All three activities below are included in the entrance ticket. On arrival, show your ticket at the yard gate and collect a paper plan. There is no mobile signal inside the mill.
Meet the Millers | 9.45 and 13.45 | 35 minutes
Follow a working miller from the sacks of grain on the ground floor to the great stones above. The tour involves two steep flights of stairs. Book a place online before Friday evening. Arrive ten minutes early, as the group enters the working area together.
Flour Lab | 10.30 to 12.30 | about 25 minutes
At a table in the yard, compare three flours and try turning a small stone mill by hand. Groups start whenever a table becomes free. Put your name on the list at the table on Saturday morning. If the yard is wet, the activity moves to the cart shed beside the gate.
Mill on Film | 11.00, 12.00 and 14.00 | 20 minutes
Our film follows one sack of grain through the upper rooms. The ground-floor cinema has level access from the yard. Seats cannot be reserved. Doors open five minutes before each showing.
Bringing a picnic? The orchard beyond the yard is open until 15.00. Please keep your entrance ticket if you go out there, as you will need it to come back through the gate.

B.title: B
B.text:
My first paid job in a theatre was to paint a kitchen wall. On the stage floor lay a wooden frame covered with cloth. Vera, the designer, wanted the cloth to look like the brick wall of an old bakery. By lunch I had finished a square of perhaps thirty bricks. Each had its own tiny cracks. I had even painted a thin green line where the wall would have met the ground.
Vera pulled two chairs to the back of the hall. From there I could just make out a dark patch the size of a suitcase. She handed me a brush nearly as wide as my hand. I thought of my little cracks and said, rather sharply, "I suppose you'd like it done by tea?"
"It would help," she said. "But that's not why."
We went back to the cloth. She dipped the big brush in brown paint and dragged it almost dry across three rows at once. I could have done that blindfolded. Then she asked me to take the two chairs back down the aisle while she switched on the stage lights. From the same seats I saw a long mark that might have been left by a shelf, and above it the pale patches where jars had stood for years. The little cracks were still there. I knew because I had painted them.
On opening night a girl sitting beside me whispered to her father, "They've taken the bread down." There was no bread in the script. For the rest of the scene I found myself wondering who had moved it and why. When the lights came up, my father, on my other side, asked which part I had painted. I could have pointed out my square. Instead I pointed to the pale strip running halfway across the kitchen. "We had a shelf there once," I told him.

C.title: C
C.text:
At a sailing club, new members learn to tie a particular knot by watching a short film. The instructor's hands fill the screen. One end of the rope goes behind the other, disappears for a second and comes out through a loop. Beginners often stop the film just before the end disappears. The club's teaching group wondered whether the pause button was doing more than simply making the lesson longer.
The group invited beginners to work in pairs in separate rooms. Which member went first was decided by drawing a name. The first learner could pause the film whenever they wished, but could not go back. The second saw a recording of exactly what had appeared on the first learner's screen, including every pause. Both had a rope and could practise throughout. After the film, almost everyone could copy the knot with the red end on the left, as it had been on screen.
Then the instructor handed each learner a rope with the red end on the right. More of those who had controlled the film tied the knot correctly this time. An observer noticed that one of these learners turned the rope in her hands before she started. "I was looking for the bit that was about to disappear," she explained. Her partner had spent the same long pause trying to pull his loose end straight.
The two beginners had watched identical pictures for the same number of seconds. Yet the frozen picture had arrived in response to a question for one of them and in the middle of a quite different difficulty for the other. There is another possibility, however. Just knowing that she could stop the film might have encouraged the first learner to predict the next move more often, even when she let the film run. The club kept the button. It also began asking learners watching together to tell their partners what they wanted to see before anyone pressed it.

D.title: D
D.text:
Every evening at six, a bakery near my flat sells a paper bag of whatever is left on its shelves. The contents are a surprise. One Tuesday I carried home five brown rolls, a lemon cake and something I eventually identified as an onion pie. A card by the till said the shop had halved its bread waste in a month. I had seen the nearly empty shelves, so I believed it. Then, on Friday, I found two of those rolls at the bottom of my bag.
What worried me was a small journey taken by the word "waste". At the shop it meant bread the baker had to throw away. By the time I read the card I had understood it to mean bread that nobody ate. It was perfectly possible for the first figure to fall faster than the second. Of my five rolls, three had become lunches, but the other two had simply changed bins.
Asking customers how much they throw away would help, although the answers could be as misleading as the empty shelves. Imagine leaving a pile of cards by the door for willing customers to fill in. A man who has turned yesterday's loaf into a fine pudding may be rather more eager to tell his story than someone who left a bag unopened on the bus. Fifty cheerful replies would still leave us wondering about the people who walked straight past.
I would keep selling the bags. Mine cost less than buying the things separately, and I enjoyed finding a use for the pie. I would change the notice, though. Say how much less bread the shop itself throws away, then invite customers chosen by chance to keep a brief record of what happens at home. Even a modest set of such records, with a note of how many people declined, would tell a reader where the good news ends and the unanswered question begins.

S.title: 七选五
S.text:
阅读下面短文，从短文后的选项中选出可以填入空白处的最佳选项。选项中有两项为多余选项。
Looking Again at a Familiar Walk
Ask me what I passed between my flat and the bus stop this morning and I can give you a shopping list: two streets, one garden, a corner shop. Ask me the shape of the shop window and I'm suddenly in trouble. [36] _____ Next time you take a familiar walk, try carrying a pencil and a small piece of paper.
Choose one spot where you can stand comfortably for a minute. Give your sketch a boundary before you put anything inside it. [37] _____ Everything outside that little square can wait for another day. Otherwise a five-minute walk can easily turn into a project you never start.
Now suppose you've chosen a doorway. We all carry a simple picture of a door in our heads, usually a tall, neat rectangle. [38] _____ Does its top actually run level with the bottom of the window beside it? Let what you see settle the question, even if the result on your page looks rather odd.
You can also write on your drawing. Perhaps the person who has just opened the door is already halfway down the street. [39] _____ A note such as "green sleeve, a bunch of keys" can bring the moment back later.
Keep the paper and stop at the same spot on another morning. This time, do a quick sketch before unfolding the first one. [40] _____ Is the doorway narrower today, or did the bicycle leaning beside it make you draw it differently?

options.A: There is no need to chase them with your pencil.
options.B: Set that ready-made picture aside and compare two edges.
options.C: The shopkeeper may be able to tell you how old the door is.
options.D: Recognising a place, it seems, is a good deal easier than seeing it.
options.E: With the two drawings side by side, small differences begin to show.
options.F: It might take in just what you can see between two posts of a fence.
options.G: Give the completed sketch to someone who has never taken that walk.

T.title: 完形填空
T.text:
阅读下面短文，从每题所给的 A、B、C、D 四个选项中选出可以填入空白处的最佳选项。
On the first Saturday of the junior chess tournament, I ran the results desk. I had made a chart with a tidy square for every score. By lunchtime every square was filled except one. I went looking for the [41] _____ game.
Two boys were still at their board, although the hall was almost [42] _____. The other players had gone upstairs for lunch. As I drew closer, the smaller boy knocked his own king over. I reached for my pen. Then the other boy stood the king up and put two captured pieces [43] _____ where they had been. They started again.
"Which one of you won?" I asked. Both pointed at the taller boy. "About twenty minutes ago," he said. So why were they still [44] _____?
The smaller boy had been one move from a win himself, or so he [45] _____. He wanted to find out. His opponent had [46] _____ to put the pieces where they had been just before the mistake. But each remembered the position a little [47] _____. Now they were trying both versions.
I wrote down the score and told them I needed their table for the next round. The little boy began to [48] _____ the pieces. His opponent held out a hand to stop him. "Where can we finish this?" he asked me.
Beside my desk stood a small table. It was meant to [49] _____ the prizes. I moved the silver cups to the windowsill. The boys carried their board across the room, slowly enough to keep the pieces in [50] _____.
By afternoon, players who had finished their games were [51] _____ around the small table, waiting for a turn to try a move again. Nobody asked me to [52] _____ those games. When a parent asked who was [53] _____ at my new table, I couldn't tell her.
Next time I drew up the hall plan, I marked a space beside the desk before I even counted the competition boards. But when I drew up the results chart, I [54] _____ that table. A good game, I had discovered, doesn't always end when the score is [55] _____.

U.title: 语法填空
U.text:
阅读下面短文，在空白处填入适当的单词或括号内单词的正确形式，每空限填一词。
In the print room of a small museum, a wooden drawer stands open on the counter. Inside it are rows of tiny wooden blocks, each [56] _____ (carry) a single letter. The letters look strange until you see an impression on paper. A printer must arrange them back to front so that the words will appear the right way round.
Last winter, the museum [57] _____ (receive) the drawer from a family printing business when its owner retired. One block printed such [58] _____ unusually large question mark that it would scarcely fit on a postcard. A photograph tucked beneath the drawer showed it on a poster for a village play. The actor [59] _____ name appeared below the mark was the owner's grandfather.
Visitors can now make a card of their own. They choose three [60] _____ (word) and set them in a frame. Before [61] _____ (add) ink, they check the letters in a mirror. One child set the type so carefully that her print matched the guide’s sample [62] _____ (exact), right down to a hairline gap. Many visitors take pride [63] _____ the little differences between their prints. Three impressions from the same block hang by the door: one is pale grey, one is almost black and one is jet black. Of the three, the last is the [64] _____ (dark). For many visitors, that small difference is precisely what makes the card worth [65] _____ (keep).

V.title: 读后续写
V.text:
On the morning we were moving out of our flat, my little sister May went missing. I found her in the kitchen with her back against the pantry door. A pair of bare feet stuck out from under her yellow raincoat, although it was a perfectly dry day.
"What are you doing?" I asked.
"Being four," she said. Then she stood on tiptoe. "Now I'm nearly six."
I knew what she meant. For every birthday Dad had stood us against that white door and drawn a line above our heads. Beside each line he had written a name and a date. There was a shaky red one where May had tried to measure me herself. The highest blue line was mine, made only last week. With the coats and pictures gone, that door looked more like us than anything else in the flat.
In the sitting room, Dad was folding the last empty box. Our new flat was only three streets away, but he had been carrying boxes up and down stairs since breakfast. When May asked him to take the door, he put the box down. "The next family will need somewhere to keep their food too," he said. "I'll give you five minutes before we lock up."
I took a picture of the marks with my phone. May looked at the screen, set the phone against the wall and tried to stand beside her red line. In the picture the whole door was shorter than her hand. She handed it back without a word.
Outside, the van driver sounded his horn. Dad went down to tell him we were nearly ready. Looking around the bare room, I noticed a roll of brown packing paper behind the bin. The white tape we'd used to close the boxes was still round my wrist.

listening.L01:
W: Are those the posters for the match? I can put one up in the dining hall on my way to lunch.
M: Thanks, but look at the date. These are the old ones. The new design is on my screen, waiting for someone to fill the printer with paper.
W: I'll get some from the office.
listening.L02:
M: I was going to catch the ten-fifteen train. That would give us ages before the concert at twelve.
W: It doesn't run on Sundays, remember? The next one's at eleven. If you meet me on the platform at a quarter to eleven, we'll have time to get seats.
M: See you there, then.
listening.L03:
W: I know you wanted to borrow my blue jacket for your picture. I'm wearing it to work, I'm afraid.
M: Never mind. They only need a picture of my face for the card. I'll go as I am.
listening.L04:
M: That last bend on the river looked black in your painting. Did you run out of blue?
W: I had plenty. I wanted you to look first at the bright little boat. If I'd made the water bright too, you'd hardly have noticed it.
listening.L05:
W: Are you coming down for a slice of cake? It's Ben's last day.
M: Save me one, will you? I've got someone on the other line. She's been waiting for me to check her booking.
W: I'll tell Ben you'll be along in a minute.
listening.L06:
M: Did you find the missing page from the school magazine, Nia?
W: It was there the whole time, Sam. Two pages had stuck together. But I'm glad I checked. The photo under the heading "Spring Show" is of the winter concert.
M: Can't we change the heading?
W: Look at the article underneath. It's about the spring dancers. We need a different picture.
M: I took one from the front row. Shall I send it?
W: Please, in its original size. I can cut the edges off here. And don't worry about writing a line for it; the dancers have already sent their names.
listening.L07:
W: Is the round table by the window still for sale?
M: It is. I put it online yesterday. It's forty pounds, or fifty if I bring it round in my van.
W: My brother has a car. The problem is getting it through the narrow door at my flat. Can the legs come off?
M: Yes. I took them off when I moved here. There's a little bag of spare screws underneath.
W: Lovely. My brother finishes work at six, so we could come about seven.
M: Fine. It's a turning off King Street. People usually stop at the green door because my address is number nine, but that's the front of the house. Drive round to the blue gate. I'll bring it out there.
W: Good. I'll bring the forty in cash.
listening.L08:
M: How was your first morning at the radio station, Grace? Were you on air?
W: Only my left shoe! They were recording a play, and they needed someone walking upstairs. I crossed the studio in my trainers. It sounded as if I was walking on a carpet.
M: Wasn't the scene set in a hotel?
W: Yes, but the stairs were supposed to be bare wood. A man gave me a pair of hard shoes and a short board to walk on. The sound was right, only I was walking too fast.
M: How did you know?
W: The actress was out of breath when she reached the top in the story. At my speed she'd have been there before she even started speaking. So I watched her hand. She raised a finger each time she wanted another step.
M: Will you get to speak next time?
W: They've asked me back to make rain. After this morning I'm rather curious to find out what they use.
listening.L09:
W: Before we open the little bookstall, Mr Reed, can I check how the prices work? The sign says two pounds for paperbacks, three for hardbacks.
M: That's for this first hour. After eleven, everything on the left table is a pound. The right table stays as it is. Most of the children's books are there.
W: And those books under your chair?
M: A teacher asked for books about the sea. I chose six for her school. She hasn't seen them yet. Would you keep them there until she comes?
W: Certainly. Do I give people one of these cards when they buy something?
M: Only if they ask about giving us books. The address of our store is printed on the back. For today's sale, people can just choose their books and pay you.
W: What if somebody wants to pay with a card?
M: Send them to me at the right table. Here's some change for cash sales.
listening.L10:
W: If you're here for the first time, welcome to the North Street Swimming Club. I'm June and I look after the club records. Three years ago I found a tin full of little brass discs in the old office. At first I thought they were medals. Then I noticed the same numbers appeared over and over again, but never a swimmer's name. An older member showed me a picture of the changing room in the 1970s. You can just see a boy handing a disc to the woman behind the counter. She kept swimmers' clothes in numbered baskets. The discs were how people got their own clothes back.
We'd like to put that photograph in our entrance hall. The trouble is, the person who took it is still unknown. If you know who stood behind the camera, come and see me after the meeting. Several people have already told us the boy's name, so that part is settled. Next month we're having an open afternoon. You're welcome to bring old photographs then. We'll make copies on the spot and you can take the originals home the same day.
